\section{Bureau Visibility and Affordability Screening}
\label{sec:scenarios}

% Every number is read from thesis/chapters/generated/tab_scenarios.tex (results/raw/rq3s.parquet,
% 100 replicates per arm), tab_cooloff.tex or tab_cap.tex, or from
% results/summary/results_numbers.json, all generated by notebooks/scripts/build_results_tables.py.

This section answers RQ3. The benchmark is the position before the reporting arrangements.
Under bureau visibility, \ac{BNPL} obligations enter the traditional lender's
Regulation 23A test, which is how we model the reported bureau arrangements
\cite{businessday_bnpl_2026}. Under mandatory screening, the same test is applied to every
\ac{BNPL} request, a stricter version of the \ac{FCA}'s affordability check
\cite{fca_ps26_1, woolard2021}. A third arm combines both (Section~\ref{sec:asymmetry}). Each
arm runs at $\beta=0$ and $\beta=1$ with one hundred replicates on shared seeds, so a
difference of 0.08 points in default is detected about half the time and one of 0.12 points
usually.
% switch_se_max = 0.0004, switch_detectable_min = 0.0008 in results_numbers.json.

Neither switch lowers default (Table~\ref{tab:scenarios}; Figure~\ref{fig:scenarios}). Bureau
visibility raises it, by $0.18 \pm 0.03$ points at $\beta=0$ and $0.16 \pm 0.03$ at
$\beta=1$. Screening changes it by $+0.04 \pm 0.03$ and $+0.02 \pm 0.03$ points, which is not
detectable, although a rise of about a tenth of a point cannot be ruled out.

Bureau visibility works through refusals. Once the lender sees \ac{BNPL} instalments, it
refuses about 15\% more applications and lends 12 to 14\% less. What it sees is almost entirely
live instalments: arrears and late fees are under 0.5\% of the visible obligation, because
nearly all \ac{BNPL} arrears belong to households that have already defaulted and no longer
apply. Between 27 and 30\% of the obligation is on agreements opened in the same
tick against the same shortfall, which a bureau reporting with a lag would not show.
% arrears_share_at_application (0.0028, 0.0045; at most 0.021 in any quintile),
% arrears_held_by_defaulted_share (0.999) and live_opened_same_tick_share_at_application
% (0.30, 0.27) in results/summary/bureau_visible_split.json
% (notebooks/scripts/check_bureau_visible_split.py, seeds 80,000-80,019).
A refused household in the
model has no other source of credit, so its unmet debt service is distress in that tick, and
it has no loan left to save against the next tick's food and rent (Section~\ref{sec:sequence}). Default rises most in Q1, the poorest quintile, by
$0.44 \pm 0.06$ points at $\beta=0$ and $0.54 \pm 0.05$ at $\beta=1$, and detectably also in
Q2 and Q3 at $\beta=0$ only. \ac{BNPL} volume falls by less than 3\%, because the switch acts
on traditional lending and not on \ac{BNPL} requests.
% 15%: +161/1060 and +164/1073 refusals; 12 to 14%: lever_bureau_beta{0,1}_lending_diff over
% lever_bench_beta{0,1}_lending (-0.120, -0.142).

The model's rules may favour this result. A refusal can cause distress at once, whereas a granted
loan is repaid over 25 months, partly after the run ends, and the lender assesses surveyed
rather than current income. Under the rule in which a loan that pays food and rent clears that
tick's distress (Section~\ref{sec:results-effect}), a refusal becomes almost the only route into
distress, and the rise is larger: $0.40 \pm 0.01$ and $0.42 \pm 0.01$ points from a benchmark of
4.4\%, most in Q1, while screening changes default by at most 0.02 points. The switches were not run under the other rules of Table~\ref{tab:effect} or
over a longer horizon, so the result gives the direction of the affordability channel and is not
a forecast.
% rq3r_bench_default_b{0,1}, rq3r_bureau_default_diff_b{0,1} (+ _se), rq3r_bureau_default_diff_Q*,
% rq3r_afford_default_diff_b{0,1} in results/summary/results_numbers.json (suite rq3r, seeds
% 80,000-80,099, 100 replicates).

Screening reduces \ac{BNPL} use: holding at the final tick falls by 1.4 points at $\beta=0$
and 2.4 at $\beta=1$, and volume by 4.6\% and 1.2\%. Its one detectable effect on default is in
Q4, $+0.23 \pm 0.09$ and $+0.24 \pm 0.09$ points on the same seeds, the quintile discussed in
Section~\ref{sec:results-distribution}. Default may not move because a \ac{BNPL} agreement is
small beside the room the Regulation 23A test allows, because the test is applied before the
income shocks that drive distress, or because a refused shortfall request passes in full to the
traditional lender (Algorithm~\ref{alg:gate}); we tested none of these.

With both switches, default is 0.06 points above the benchmark at each $\beta$, which is not
detectable. Against visibility alone, adding screening lowers default by $0.13 \pm 0.03$ points
at $\beta=0$ and $0.10 \pm 0.03$ at $\beta=1$, and roughly halves the extra refusals. Screening
may refuse \ac{BNPL} to households near the Regulation 23A limit, whose \ac{BNPL} instalments
would otherwise lead the traditional lender to refuse them. This is not tested.
Peer influence raises default by 0.18 to 0.21 points in every arm but does not detectably
change the effect of either switch ($-0.02 \pm 0.05$ points for bureau visibility).
% switch_both_less_bureau_beta{0,1} (+ _se); switch_{bench,bureau,afford,both}_beta_gap;
% switch_bureau_interaction (+ _se), results/summary/results_numbers.json.

Two further levers, a cooling-off window of one to four ticks after a want-driven purchase and
a hypothetical cap on platforms owed, are reported in Appendix~\ref{app:levers}. Of their
fourteen contrasts with the benchmark, chance alone would make about one detectable, and two
are: the two-tick window at $\beta=0$, $+0.15 \pm 0.06$ points, which the windows either side
do not support, and the four-tick window at $\beta=1$, $-0.21 \pm 0.07$ points. No cap lowers
default by more than about 0.1 points.

In answer to RQ3, making \ac{BNPL} instalments visible to the traditional lender raises
default, most in the poorest quintile, because refused households have nowhere else to borrow.
Mandatory screening does not change default detectably, but added to visibility it removes
about two-thirds of visibility's rise. Neither switch lowers aggregate default.
